Between 2019 and 2020, EI programs in RI reported a 33% average of staff turnover, with the highest turnover for Early Interventionist I (the lowest paid position in EI).
Due to the shortage of qualified applicants for Early Interventionist II positions, programs in RI such as Meeting Street are offering signing bonus to recruit applicants.
In terms of overall need for these services, there was an 88% delay or interruption of services to children due to staff turnover and shortages, as well as 88% of families withdrawing from EI services due to staff challenges and turnover in 2021 (RI KidsCount, 2021).
This shortage of qualified early intervention personnel places children in Rhode Island at higher risk for developing delays and/or disabilities.
Studies indicate that the severe staff shortage has made it difficult for Early Intervention programs to accept all children in need of help (Nesi & Sherman, 2022).
In terms of state competition, Rhode Island College currently offers two options: a master’s degree in Early Childhood Special Education and an Early Intervention Certificate program.

The master program includes course work designed to enhance specific knowledge of Early Intervention: a course on working with families in EI, and a required internship in EI.
Other course work addresses develop and assessment of young children (birth through age 8) with special needs.
The inclusion of EI related courses in the Masters was designed to increase skills and interest relative to EI.
However, pay scales differences between public educational systems and EI programs appear to dampen enthusiasm for the EI jobs.
RIC’s EI certificate is designed and limited to current EI employees who have at least two years in EI and are seeking to advance in EI.
In contrast, the URI Certificate in Early Intervention is targeted to undergraduates and therefore does not conflict with either RIC programs instead, it creates an additional pathway to become qualified personnel in EI.
The only regional competitor is Northeastern University.
Northeastern offers a Certificate in Early Intervention, with coursework similar to URI’s EI certificate proposal, that the state of Massachusetts has approved for provisional certification with advanced standing (PCAS) in Early Intervention.

Applicants who possess the PCAS must then complete 1440 hours of supervised employment in an EI setting before applying for permanent standing.
It is likely that the proposed certificate in EI at URI would allow graduates to obtain this provisional certification in Massachusetts.
